Supabase’s free tier is intended for experimentation and small projects, so hitting the storage ceiling is common. Here are the practical options you can weigh: | What to do | What it means | Pros | Cons | |------------|---------------|------|------| | **Delete older, unneeded rows** | Remove data that you’ve archived elsewhere (e.g. a CSV file or your own backup) | • Fastest way to free up space
• No cost | • Data loss if you don’t have a backup
• You’ll need to keep the backup in a reliable place | | **Archive data elsewhere** | Export to a CSV/JSON file and store it in a cloud bucket (S3, Google Drive, etc.) | • Retain the data for future reference | • Extra step to export & upload
• You’ll still need “free” storage at the source until you move it away | | **Delete & keep snapshots** | Use Supabase’s “Backups” feature (available on paid plans) or take a DB dump yourself in a safe location | • Easy rollback if you delete something by mistake | • Requires a paid plan (free tier doesn’t expose automatic backups) | | **Upgrade your plan** | Move to a paid tier (Starter, Pro…) that offers more database storage | • No need to delete or archive anything
• More room for future growth | • Cost – you’ll be paying monthly/annual fees | | **Restructure your data** | Move some large blobs or logs to Supabase Storage buckets (they’re separate from the DB size) | • Frees up DB space without deleting
• Keeps data in Supabase ecosystem | • Requires some refactoring in your code | | **Split the project** | Keep only the most critical tables in the free DB; export or archive the others | • Keeps a “lite” project in free tier | • Maintenance overhead + sync issues | ### Quick sanity‑check 1. **How much space do you have left?** In the Supabase dashboard → **Project Settings → Database**. 2. **Export before deleting**: ```bash pg_dump -t your_table_name --column-inserts your_db_name > backup.sql ``` or use the Supabase “Export Data” UI if it’s available. 3. **Delete with a temp flag**: Instead of hard‑deleting, add a column `archived_at` and set it for old rows. Then run a query like: ```sql DELETE FROM your_table WHERE archived_at IS NOT NULL AND archived_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'; ``` This gives you a safe rollback window and keeps the history. ### Bottom line If you’re happy to lose that old data or can reliably back it up elsewhere, deleting is fine and will instantly free up space. If you think you might need that data later, first export it, then delete. If you plan to grow the project or need the data always‑available, consider upgrading to a paid plan. Let me know which approach sounds most reasonable for your use case, and I can walk you through the exact commands or interface steps!
